title: The bathhouse
hookLine: public baths near mosques, for cleanliness and community

cards: Steam, first. Then the sounds: water poured from a metal bowl onto stone, voices echoing under a low dome pierced with small round windows of glass, so the light comes down in coins.

Someone is scrubbing someone else's back. Someone is lying on a warm marble slab, staring up at the coins of light. Outside, a few steps away, the market is loud and the mosque is waiting for the next prayer.
Today: the bathhouse. The word is hammam.

teach.b: Washing sits close to the heart of Muslim practice. Before prayer comes wudu: washing the face, the hands and arms, wiping the head, and then the feet, as surah five of the Qur'an sets out.
Sunni Muslims wash the feet; Shia Muslims read the same verse as asking them to wipe. After certain states, such as sex or menstruation, comes ghusl, a full bath.
A saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in Sahih Muslim calls purity half of faith. Another, in Sahih al-Bukhari, asks those coming to Friday prayer to bathe first.
And the Qur'an says that God loves those who turn to Him, and loves those who keep themselves clean. So in a town where houses had no running water, a public bath wasn't a luxury.

teach.h: A TOWN GETTING READY TO PRAY.
teach.b: It was where the town got ready to pray. Hammams were built near mosques and markets. Some were endowed as waqf, and their fees helped pay for the mosque or school next door.
Inside, a path from cool to warm to hot, and back again. Men and women went at separate hours or to separate baths. And the hammam was more than washing.
Neighbors met there. Before a wedding, or after a birth, families came with food and music. People also tell of mothers looking over the young women at the baths for a bride for their sons.
There were limits too: a hadith collected by al-Tirmidhi tells men to enter only with a waist cloth.

teach.h: STRICT ABOUT BODIES, GENEROUS WITH COMPANY.
teach.b: The hammam held both: strict about the body, generous with company.

how: Muslims make wudu before prayer and ghusl after major impurity and, by custom, before Friday prayer; historic hammams are still in use in cities such as Istanbul, Fez, Cairo and Damascus, with separate hours or sections for men and women.

o: a full bath taken at home after certain states
a public bathhouse, near the mosque and the market
the washing before prayer: face, hands, head, feet

p: purity, in a hadith in Sahih Muslim
a bathhouse by the mosque and market

s: the hammam was only about getting clean
neighbors met there, and families came with food and music before weddings and after births.
the Qur'an says Allah loves those who care for cleanness
men and women bathed together in the hammam

games.q: you live in an old city with no running water at home, and it's almost time for Friday prayer. where do you go first?
o: to the hammam, then the mosque.
games.why: a hadith in al-Bukhari asks those coming to Friday prayer to bathe first. the hammam, a few steps from the mosque, was where a town got ready.

practice: Wash your hands and face slowly now, or simply imagine it, and feel the water's temperature: the hands, then the face, then the back of the neck, where it feels cool and where it warms.
If you pray, you can make it your wudu, with intention; if you don't, let it be a slow, careful wash.

wordCard.voice: Hammam. The public bathhouse near the mosque and the market, for cleanliness and for company. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: clean together. A town getting ready to pray, side by side. See you tomorrow.
